question_text: How does the height of the tropopause normally vary with latitude in the northern hemisphere ?
option_a: It decreases from south to north.
option_b: It remains constant from north to south.
option_c: It increases from south to north.
option_d: It remains constant throughout the year.
explanation: The height of the tropopause decreases from south to north (equator to pole) in the Northern Hemisphere due to the decreasing temperature of the troposphere.

question_text: What, approximately, is the average height of the tropopause over the equator ?
explanation: The average height of the tropopause over the equator is approximately 16 km, where strong solar heating and convection push it to its highest level.

question_text: In which layer is most of the atmospheric humidity concentrated ?
explanation: Most of the atmospheric water vapor and humidity is concentrated in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere where active weather occurs.

question_text: What is the boundary layer between troposphere and stratosphere called?
explanation: The tropopause is the transition boundary layer that separates the troposphere below from the stratosphere above.

question_text: Which of the following cloud types can project up into the stratosphere?
explanation: Only Cumulonimbus (Cb) clouds possess the violent vertical development necessary to penetrate the tropopause and project up into the stratosphere.

question_text: Which one of the following statements applies to the tropopause?
option_a: It separates the troposphere from the stratosphere
option_b: It is, by definition, an isothermal layer
option_c: It indicates a strong temperature lapse rate
option_d: It is, by definition, a temperature inversion
explanation: The tropopause is the boundary layer that separates the troposphere from the stratosphere, marked by a change in temperature lapse rate.

question_text: Which layer of the atmosphere contains more than 90 per cent of all water vapour?
explanation: The troposphere contains more than 90% of all water vapor in the atmosphere, as it is directly fed by evaporation from the surface.

question_text: The thickness of the troposphere varies with
explanation: The thickness of the troposphere varies primarily with latitude, being thickest at the equator due to warm air expansion and thinnest at the poles.

question_text: What is the approximate composition of the dry air by volume in the troposphere ?
option_a: 21 % oxygen, 78 % nitrogen, and the rest other gasses
option_b: 10 % oxygen, 89 % nitrogen, and the rest other gasses
option_c: 88 % oxygen, 9 % nitrogen, and the rest other gasses
option_d: 50 % oxygen, 40 % nitrogen, and the rest other gasses
explanation: Dry air in the troposphere is composed of approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% of other gases (primarily argon and carbon dioxide).

question_text: Going from the equator to the north pole, the altitude of the tropopause
explanation: Traveling from the equator to the north pole, the tropopause altitude decreases (from 16 km to 8 km) and its temperature increases (from -75°C to -40°C).

question_text: The troposphere
option_a: has a greater vertical extent above the equator than above the poles
option_b: contains all oxygen of the stratosphere
option_c: is the separation layer between the stratosphere and atmosphere
option_d: reaches the same height at all latitudes
explanation: The troposphere is characterized by vertical air currents and has a much greater vertical extent above the equator than above the poles.

question_text: The troposphere is the
option_a: part of the atmosphere below the tropopause
option_b: part of the atmosphere above the stratosphere
option_c: boundary between the mesosphere and thermosphere
option_d: boundary between the stratosphere and the mesosphere
explanation: The troposphere is defined as the lowest part of the atmosphere, extending from the Earth's surface up to the tropopause boundary.

question_text: The tropopause is a level at which
option_a: temperature ceases to fall with increasing height
explanation: The tropopause is defined as the level where the environmental temperature ceases to fall with increasing height, marking the start of an isothermal layer.

question_text: The tropopause is lower
option_a: over the North Pole than over the equator
option_b: in summer than winter in moderate latitudes
option_c: south of the equator than north of it
option_d: over the equator than over the South Pole
explanation: The tropopause is lower over the North Pole (where cold air compresses the troposphere) than over the equator (where warm air expands it).

question_text: The average height of the tropopause at 50°N is about
explanation: In the mid-latitudes (around 50°N), the average height of the tropopause is approximately 11 km (about 36,000 feet).

question_text: The height and the temperature of the tropopause are respectively in the order of
explanation: Over the equator, the tropopause is characterized by a high altitude of about 16 km and an extremely low temperature of about -75°C.

question_text: In the mid-latitudes the stratosphere extends on an average from
explanation: In the mid-latitudes, the stratosphere extends on average from the tropopause (around 11 km) up to the stratopause (around 50 km).

question_text: The temperature at FL 140 is -12°C. What will the temperature be at FL 110 if the ICAO standard lapse rate is applied ?
explanation: Applying the ICAO standard lapse rate of 2°C per 1000 ft, a 3000 ft descent from FL 140 (-12°C) to FL 110 will increase temperature by 6°C to -6°C.

question_text: At a certain position, the temperature on the 300 hPa chart is -48°C, according to the tropopause chart, the tropopause is at FL 330. What is the most likely temperature at FL 350 ?
explanation: At FL 350 (above the tropopause at FL 330), the temperature remains nearly constant or slightly increases, making -50°C the most likely value.

question_text: An outside air temperature of -35°C is measured while cruising at FL 200. What is the temperature deviation from the ISA at this level?
explanation: At FL 200, the standard temperature is -25°C. A measured temperature of -35°C represents a deviation of 10°C colder than ISA.

question_text: What is the most likely temperature at the tropical tropopause?
explanation: The tropopause is coldest over the equator, reaching a typical temperature of approximately -75°C due to strong vertical expansion.

question_text: The 0° isotherm is forecast to be at FL 50. At what FL would you expect a temperature of -6° C?
explanation: With a standard lapse rate of 2°C/1000 ft, a temperature of -6°C (6°C colder than standard 0°C at FL 50) is found 3000 ft higher at FL 80.

question_text: The temperature at FL 80 is +6°C. What will the temperature be at FL 130 if the ICAO standard lapse rate is applied ?
explanation: From FL 80 to FL 130 is an increase of 5000 ft. Applying the lapse rate of 2°C/1000 ft (10°C drop) to +6°C yields -4°C.

question_text: The temperature at FL 110 is -5°C. What will the temperature be at FL 50 if the ICAO standard lapse rate is applied ?
explanation: From FL 110 to FL 50 is a descent of 6000 ft. Applying the lapse rate of 2°C/1000 ft (12°C rise) to -5°C yields +7°C.

question_text: The temperature at FL 160 is -22°C. What will the temperature be at FL 90 if the ICAO standard lapse rate is applied ?
explanation: From FL 160 to FL 90 is a descent of 7000 ft. Applying the lapse rate of 2°C/1000 ft (14°C rise) to -22°C yields -8°C.

question_text: A temperature of +15°C is recorded at an altitude of 500 metres above sea level. If the vertical temperature gradient is that of a standard atmosphere, what will the temperature be at the summit of a mountain, 2500 metres above sea level?
explanation: A height increase of 2000m at the standard lapse rate of 0.65°C/100m yields a 13°C drop, reducing 15°C at 500m to 2°C at 2500m.

question_text: How would you characterise an air temperature of -15°C at the 700 hPa level over western Europe?
explanation: At 700 hPa (approx 10,000 ft), standard temp is -5°C. A temperature of -15°C represents a significant negative deviation, which is low.

question_text: How would you characterise an air temperature of -30°C at the 300 hPa level over western Europe?
explanation: At 300 hPa (approx 30,000 ft), standard temp is -45°C. A temperature of -30°C represents a significant positive deviation, which is high.

question_text: How would you characterise an air temperature of -55°C at the 200 hPa level over western Europe?
explanation: At 200 hPa (approx 39,000 ft), the standard temperature is -56.5°C, meaning a measured temperature of -55°C is within +/-5°C of ISA.

question_text: In the lower part of the stratosphere the temperature
option_d: increases at first and decreases afterward
explanation: In the lower part of the stratosphere, temperature is almost constant (isothermal) before beginning to increase at higher altitudes.

question_text: Which is true of the temperature at the tropopause?
option_a: It is higher in polar regions than in equatorial regions
option_b: It is higher in equatorial regions than in polar regions
option_c: It is highest in middle latitudes
option_d: There is no significant difference with change of latitude
explanation: The tropopause temperature is higher in polar regions (approx -45°C) than in equatorial regions (approx -75°C) due to height differences.

question_text: Several physical processes contribute to atmospheric warming. Which of the following contribute the most ?
explanation: Convection (vertical movement of air) and condensation (latent heat release) are the primary processes that warm the atmosphere from the ground.

question_text: Convective activity over land in mid-latitudes is greatest in
option_b: winter during the night and early morning.
option_c: summer during the night and early morning.
explanation: Convective activity over land is greatest during summer afternoons when solar radiation has heated the surface to its maximum diurnal temperature.

question_text: Advection is :
explanation: Advection is the term used to describe the horizontal movement of air or air mass properties.

question_text: The radiation of the sun heats
option_a: the surface of the earth, which heats the air in the troposphere
option_b: the air in the troposphere directly
option_c: the water vapour in the air of the troposphere
option_d: the air in the troposphere only directly if no clouds are present
explanation: Solar radiation passes through the atmosphere and heats the Earth's surface, which then heats the adjacent tropospheric air from below.

question_text: A layer is conditionally unstable if the air
option_a: is unstable for saturated air and stable for dry air.
option_b: is stable for saturated air and unstable for dry air.
option_d: is unstable for saturated air as well as for dry air.
explanation: A layer is conditionally unstable if the environmental lapse rate lies between the dry adiabatic (stable) and saturated adiabatic (unstable) lapse rates.

question_text: Absolute instability exists whenever the environmental lapse rate
option_a: exceeds the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
option_b: exceeds the saturated adiabatic lapse rate.
option_c: is less than the saturated adiabatic lapse rate.
option_d: is between the dry and saturated adiabatic lapse rate.
explanation: Absolute instability occurs when the environmental lapse rate exceeds the dry adiabatic lapse rate, meaning any air parcel will rise.

question_text: In an air mass with no clouds the surface temperature is 15°C and 13°C at 1000m. This layer of air is:
explanation: A temp drop of 2°C over 1000m (0.2°C/100m) is less than both the dry and wet adiabatic lapse rates, meaning the layer is stable.

question_text: The dry adiabatic lapse rate
option_b: is greater in summer than in winter
option_c: is greater during the night than during the day
explanation: The dry adiabatic lapse rate represents a thermodynamic constant of approximately 1°C per 100 m (or 3°C per 1000 ft).

question_text: An air mass is called stable when
option_a: the vertical motion of rising air tends to become weaker and disappears
option_b: the temperature in a given air mass decreases rapidly with height
option_c: the pressure in a given area is constant
option_d: the environmental lapse rate is high, with little vertical motion of air currents
explanation: An air mass is stable when the environmental lapse rate is small, meaning vertical air currents are suppressed and quickly disappear.

question_text: A layer can be
option_a: stable for unsaturated air and unstable for saturated air
option_b: stable for saturated air and unstable for unsaturated air
option_c: unstable for unsaturated air and neutral for saturated air
option_d: unstable for unsaturated air and conditionally unstable
explanation: A layer is conditionally unstable when it is stable for unsaturated (dry) air but unstable for saturated (wet) air.

question_text: From which of the following pieces of information can the stability of the atmosphere be derived?
explanation: The stability of a layer in the atmosphere is determined by comparing the actual environmental lapse rate to the adiabatic lapse rates.

question_text: When in the upper part of a layer warm air is advected the
option_c: wind will back with increasing height in the northern hemisphere
option_d: wind speed will always decrease with increasing height in the northern hemisphere
explanation: Advecting warm air into the upper part of a layer increases the temperature aloft, reducing the lapse rate and increasing stability.

question_text: An inversion is a layer of air which is
explanation: A temperature inversion (temperature increasing with height) has a negative lapse rate, making the layer absolutely stable.

question_text: The environmental lapse rate in an actual atmosphere
option_d: has a fixed value of 2°C/1000 FT
explanation: The environmental lapse rate is the actual vertical temperature gradient of the atmosphere, which varies dynamically with time and location.

question_text: The dry adiabatic lapse rate has a value of
explanation: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is a constant physical value of approximately 1°C per 100 m (or 3°C per 1000 ft).

question_text: In still air the temperature decreases at an average of 1.2°C per 100 m increase in altitude. This temperature change is called:
explanation: The actual change in temperature with height measured in the atmosphere at a specific time is called the environmental lapse rate.

question_text: The value of the saturated adiabatic lapse rate is closest to that of the dry adiabatic lapse rate in
explanation: The saturated adiabatic lapse rate approaches the dry adiabatic lapse rate (1°C/100m) at very low temperatures (e.g. in cirrus levels) where water vapor is minimal.

question_text: Which of the following is a common cause of ground or surface temperature inversion ?
option_a: Terrestrial radiation on a clear night with no or very light winds.
option_b: Warm air being lifted rapidly aloft, in the vicinity of mountainous terrain.
option_c: The movement of colder air under warm air, or the movement of warm air over cold air.
option_d: Heating of the air by subsidence
explanation: A ground temperature inversion is typically caused by terrestrial radiation cooling the surface on a clear night with little or no wind.

question_text: Which of the following is a common result of subsidence ?
option_a: An inversion over a large area with haze, mist.
option_b: CB-clouds and thunderstorms over a large area.
option_c: Wide spread NS and AS clouds and intense precipitation.
option_d: Clear air turbulence at higher altitudes .
explanation: Subsidence (sinking air) causes adiabatic warming aloft, creating a stable subsidence inversion that traps moisture and dust as haze or mist.

question_text: What is the technical term for an increase in temperature with altitude?
explanation: A temperature inversion is the meteorological term for an atmospheric layer in which temperature increases with altitude.

question_text: What characteristic is associated with a temperature inversion ?
explanation: A temperature inversion acts as a strong lid on vertical motion, making the layer highly stable and trapping pollutants.

question_text: A significant inversion at low height is a characteristic of
explanation: A significant low-level inversion is most commonly caused by nocturnal radiation cooling the surface under a clear sky.

question_text: An inversion is a layer of air in which the temperature
explanation: An inversion is defined as a layer of air in which the temperature increases as height increases.

question_text: An isothermal layer is a layer of air in which the temperature
option_c: decreases with height at a constant rate
option_d: increases with height at a constant rate
explanation: An isothermal layer is a layer of air in which the temperature remains constant with height (lapse rate of 0).

question_text: An inversion is
option_a: an increase of temperature with height
option_b: an increase of pressure with height
option_c: a decrease of pressure with height
option_d: a decrease of temperature with height
explanation: An inversion is characterized by an increase of air temperature with increasing height.

question_text: The diurnal variation in temperature is largest when the sky is
explanation: The diurnal temperature variation is largest when the sky is clear (maximum solar input and radiative cooling) and winds are weak (no mixing).

question_text: Around Paris on January 3rd at 1800 UTC, the surface temperature, under shelter, is 3°C. The sky is covered by 8 oktas of stratus. QNH is 1033 hPa. If the sky is covered all night, the minimum temperature of the night of January 3rd to January 4th should be
explanation: Under a thick overcast layer of stratus clouds, radiative cooling is blocked, so the night temperature will fall only slightly below 3°C.

question_text: On a clear sky, continental ground surface, wind calm, the minimum temperature is reached approximately
option_c: at the moment the sun rises
explanation: The minimum temperature on a clear night is reached shortly after sunrise because the ground continues to radiate heat until solar input builds up.

question_text: What positions are connected by isobars on the surface weather chart?
option_a: Positions with the same air pressure at a given level
option_b: Positions with the same temperature at a given level
option_c: Positions with the same wind velocity at a given level
option_d: Positions with the same relative pressure heights
explanation: Isobars are lines drawn on a weather chart connecting points of equal atmospheric pressure reduced to sea level.

question_text: The station pressure used in surface weather charts is
explanation: The station pressure reduced to sea level using actual temperature conditions is QFF, which is used on surface weather charts.

question_text: The isobars drawn on a surface weather chart represent lines of equal pressure
explanation: Isobars on a surface chart represent lines of equal pressure reduced to mean sea level (MSL) to allow comparison between stations.

question_text: Isobars on a surface chart are lines of equal
explanation: Isobars on a surface weather chart are lines of equal QFF pressure.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-10850A)The pressure distribution located mainly in square 2A is a
explanation: Looking at the pressure distribution chart, a trough of low pressure (an elongated area of relatively low pressure) is located in square 2A.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-10784A)The pressure system at position ""D"" is a
explanation: Based on the pressure chart, the pressure system located at position D represents a ridge of high pressure.

question_text: In the troposphere the decrease of pressure per 100 m increase in height
option_a: is smaller at higher levels than at lower levels.
option_c: is greater at higher levels than at lower levels.
option_d: is in the order of 27 hPa near MSL.
explanation: The rate of pressure decrease with height is directly proportional to air density; because air is less dense aloft, the decrease is smaller at higher levels.

question_text: What is the approximate vertical interval which is equal to a pressure change of 1 hPa at an altitude of 5500 m ?
explanation: At an altitude of 5500 m (approx. 500 hPa), the air is half as dense as at sea level, requiring a vertical interval of 16 m (50 ft) for a 1 hPa change.

question_text: Which of the following is true concerning atmospheric pressure ?
option_b: It is higher in winter than in summer
option_c: It is higher at night than during the day
option_d: It always decreases with height at a rate of 1 hPa per 8m
explanation: Atmospheric pressure decreases with height because the weight of the air column above decreases as altitude increases.

question_text: An isohypse (contour)
option_a: indicates the true altitude of a pressure level
option_b: is the longest slope line of a frontal surface
option_c: is the limit between two air masses of different temperature
option_d: indicates the altitude of the zero degree isotherm
explanation: An isohypse (or contour line) on an upper-level chart connects points of equal geopotential height of a constant pressure surface.

question_text: In order to calculate QFE from QNH, which of the following must be known ?
option_c: Elevation of the airfield and the temperature at MSL.
option_d: Elevation and the temperature at the airfield.
explanation: To convert QNH to QFE, the airfield elevation must be known to calculate the standard pressure difference of the air column.

question_text: The QFF at an airfield located 400 metres above sea level is 1016 hPa. The air temperature is 10°C higher than a standard atmosphere. What is the QNH?
option_d: It is not possible to give a definitive answer
explanation: Since actual temperature is warmer than standard, the actual density is lower, meaning QNH (calculated via standard temp) is higher than QFF.

question_text: The QFF at an airfield located 400 metres above sea level is 1016 hPa. The air temperature is 10°C lower than a standard atmosphere. What is the QNH?
option_d: It is not possible to give a definitive answer
explanation: When the actual temperature is colder than standard, the air column is denser, which makes QNH less than QFF.

question_text: The QNH at an airfield located 200 metres above sea level is 1009 hPa. The air temperature is 10°C lower than a standard atmosphere. What is the QFF?
option_d: It is not possible to give a definitive answer
explanation: With actual temperature colder than standard, the denser air column causes the QFF (using actual density) to be higher than QNH.

question_text: The QNH at an airfield located 200 metres above sea level is 1022 hPa. The air temperature is not available. What is the QFF?
option_a: It is not possible to give a definitive answer
explanation: Without air temperature data, it is impossible to calculate the density correction, so QFF cannot be definitively calculated from QNH.

question_text: The QNH at an airfield located 0 metres above sea level is 1022 hPa. The air temperature is not available. What is the QFF?
option_d: It is not possible to give a definitive answer
explanation: For an airfield at MSL (0 metres elevation), no elevation correction is needed, so QNH is exactly equal to QFF.

question_text: The QNH at an airfield in California located 69 metres below sea level is 1018 hPa. The air temperature is 10°C higher than a standard atmosphere. What is the QFF?
option_d: It is not possible to give a definitive answer
explanation: For an airfield below sea level in warm air, the warmer air column decreases density, making QFF greater than QNH.

question_text: The QFF at an airfield in California located 69 metres below sea level is 1030 hPa. The air temperature is 10°C lower than a standard atmosphere. What is the QNH?
option_d: It is not possible to give a definitive answer
explanation: For an airfield below sea level in cold air, the denser air column causes the calculated QNH to be greater than QFF.

question_text: If the QFE at Locarno (200 metres above sea level) is 980 hPa, what is the approximate QNH ?
explanation: At 200m elevation (approx. 25 hPa height difference), QNH is calculated by adding 25 hPa to QFE: 980 + 25 = 1005 hPa.

question_text: If the QFE at Locarno (200 metres above sea level) is 1000 hPa, what is the approximate QNH?
explanation: At 200m elevation (approx. 25 hPa height difference), QNH is calculated by adding 25 hPa to QFE: 1000 + 25 = 1025 hPa.

question_text: If the QNH at Locarno (200 metres above sea level) is 1015 hPa, what is the approximate QFE?(Assume 1hPa = 8m)
explanation: At 200m elevation (approx. 25 hPa height difference), QFE is calculated by subtracting 25 hPa from QNH: 1015 - 25 = 990 hPa.

question_text: If the QNH at Locarno (200 metres above sea level) is 1025 hPa, what is the approximate QFE?
explanation: At 200m elevation (approx. 25 hPa height difference), QFE is calculated by subtracting 25 hPa from QNH: 1025 - 25 = 1000 hPa.

question_text: QNH is defined as
option_a: QFE reduced to MSL using the values of the standard atmosphere
option_b: pressure at MSL in the standard atmosphere
option_c: pressure at MSL in the actual atmosphere
option_d: QFE reduced to MSL using the values of the actual atmosphere
explanation: QNH is defined as the station pressure (QFE) reduced to mean sea level assuming standard atmosphere temperature values.

question_text: In order to reduce QFE to QNH, which of the following item(s) must be known ?
option_c: Elevation of the airfield and the temperature at MSL
option_d: Elevation of the airfield and the temperature at the airfield
explanation: To reduce QFE to QNH, only the airfield elevation must be known, as standard atmosphere temperature parameters are used by definition.

question_text: At FL 180, the air temperature is -35°C.The air density at this level is:
option_a: Greater than the density of the ISA atmosphere at FL 180.
option_b: Less than the density of the ISA atmosphere at FL 180.
option_c: Equal to the density of the ISA atmosphere at FL 180.
option_d: Unable to be determined without knowing the QNH.
explanation: Standard temperature at FL 180 is -21°C. A temperature of -35°C is colder than standard, which increases the air density.

question_text: Under what condition does pressure altitude have the same value as density altitude ?
option_b: At sea level when the temperature is 0°C.
option_c: When the altimeter has no position error.
option_d: When the altimeter setting is 1013,2 hPa.
explanation: Density altitude equals pressure altitude under standard ISA temperature conditions, where no temperature correction is required.

question_text: Half the mass of the atmosphere is found in the first
explanation: Because air is highly compressible, about 50% of the total atmospheric mass is concentrated in the lowest 5 km of the atmosphere.

question_text: The lowest assumed temperature in the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) is :
explanation: The International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) assumes a constant minimum temperature of -56.5°C at and above the tropopause.

question_text: A 200 hPa pressure altitude level can vary in height. In temperate regions which of the following average heights is applicable ?
explanation: In temperate regions, the average height of the 200 hPa pressure level corresponds to FL 390 (approximately 39,000 feet).

question_text: A 300 hPa pressure level can vary in height. In temperate regions which of the following average heights is applicable ?
explanation: In temperate regions, the average height of the 300 hPa pressure level corresponds to FL 300 (approximately 30,000 feet).

question_text: A 500 hPa pressure level can vary in height. In temperate regions which of the following average heights is applicable ?
explanation: In temperate regions, the average height of the 500 hPa pressure level corresponds to FL 180 (approximately 18,000 feet).

question_text: A 700 hPa pressure level can vary in height. In temperate regions which of the following average heights is applicable ?
explanation: In temperate regions, the average height of the 700 hPa pressure level corresponds to FL 100 (approximately 10,000 feet).

question_text: A 850 hPa pressure level can vary in height. In temperate regions which of the following average heights is applicable ?
explanation: In temperate regions, the average height of the 850 hPa pressure level corresponds to FL 50 (approximately 5,000 feet).

question_text: If you are flying at FL 300 in an air mass that is 15°C warmer than a standard atmosphere, what is the outside temperature likely to be?
explanation: Standard temperature at FL 300 is -45°C. A +15°C temperature deviation yields an outside air temperature of -30°C.

question_text: If you are flying at FL 100 in an air mass that is 10°C warmer than a standard atmosphere, what is the outside temperature likely to be?
explanation: Standard temperature at FL 100 is -5°C. A +10°C temperature deviation yields an outside air temperature of +5°C.

question_text: If you are flying at FL 120 and the outside temperature is -2°C, at what altitude will the ""freezing level"" be?
explanation: A temperature of -2°C at FL 120 means the freezing level (0°C) is 1000 ft lower (warmer by 2°C) at FL 110.

question_text: How does temperature vary with increasing altitude in the ICAO standard atmosphere below the tropopause?
option_c: At first it increases and higher up it decreases
explanation: In the standard atmosphere, temperature decreases at a constant lapse rate of 0.65°C per 100 m up to the tropopause.

question_text: What is the vertical temperature lapse rate, up to 11 km, in the standard ICAO atmosphere ?
explanation: In the ICAO standard atmosphere, the temperature decreases at a constant lapse rate of 6.5°C per 1000 m (or 1.98°C per 1000 ft) below 11 km.

question_text: In the International Standard Atmosphere the decrease in temperature with height below 11 km is
explanation: Below 11 km in the standard atmosphere, temperature decreases at a constant rate of 0.65°C per 100 m.

question_text: Which statement is correct regarding the International Standard Atmosphere ?
option_a: At MSL temperature is 15°C and pressure is 1013.25hPa
option_b: At MSL temperature is 15°C and the decrease in temperature with height is 1°C per 100m
option_c: At MSL temperature is 10°C and the decrease in temperature with height is 1°C per 100m
option_d: At MSL pressure is 1013.25 hPa and the decrease of temperature with height is 1°C per 100m
explanation: The ICAO standard atmosphere defines mean sea level (MSL) values as a temperature of 15°C and a pressure of 1013.25 hPa.

question_text: In what hPa range is an upper weather chart for FL 340 situated?
explanation: FL 340 (34,000 ft) lies between the standard 300 hPa (~30,000 ft) and 200 hPa (~39,000 ft) upper weather charts.

question_text: The temperature at 10000 FT in the International Standard Atmosphere is :
explanation: Standard temperature at sea level is 15°C. Decreasing at 2°C per 1000 ft, the standard temperature at 10,000 ft is -5°C.

question_text: The rate of decrease of temperature with height per 100 m in the International Standard Atmosphere is :
explanation: The vertical temperature lapse rate in the standard atmosphere is a constant value of 0.65°C per 100 m (or 1.98°C per 1000 ft).

question_text: The QNH of an airport at sea level is 983 hPa and the temperature deviation from ISA is -15°C below FL 100.What is the true altitude of FL 100?
explanation: With QNH 983 hPa (30 hPa below standard, reducing true height by 810 ft) and ISA -15°C (reducing height by 6%), FL 100 true altitude is 8590 ft.

question_text: You plan a flight over a mountain range at a true altitude of 15000 FT/AMSL. The air is on an average 15°C colder than ISA, the pressure at sea level is 1003 hPa. What indication must the altimeter (setting 1013.2 hPa) read?
explanation: A true altitude of 15,000 ft in ISA -15°C air makes the altimeter overread by 6% (900 ft), and a QNH of 1003 hPa adds 300 ft, totaling 16,230 ft.

question_text: During a flight at FL 100 from Marseille (QNH 1012 hPa) to Palma de Mallorca (QNH 1015 hPa), an aircraft remains at a constant true altitude. The reason for this is that :
option_a: the air at Marseille is warmer than that at Palma de Mallorca.
option_b: the altimeters are erroneous, and need to be tested.
option_c: the air at Marseille is colder than that at Palma de Mallorca.
option_d: one of the two QNH values may be incorrect.
explanation: Palma has higher pressure than Marseille, but Marseille is warmer. The warmer air column over Marseille offsets the pressure difference, keeping true altitude constant.

question_text: You intend to overfly a mountain range. The recommended minimum flight altitude is, according to the aviation chart, 15000 FT/AMSL. The air mass that you will fly through is on average 15°C warmer than the standard atmosphere. The altimeter is set to QNH (1023 hPa). At what altimeter reading will you effectively be at the recommended minimum flight altitude?
explanation: A true altitude of 15,000 ft in ISA +15°C air makes the altimeter underread by 6% (900 ft), and a QNH of 1023 hPa offsets it, reading 14,100 ft.

question_text: You are flying at FL 130, and your true altitude is 12000 FT. What is the temperature deviation from that of the standard atmosphere at FL 130 (QNH 1013,2 hPa) ?
explanation: True altitude (12,000 ft) is 1000 ft lower than indicated (13,000 ft). A 4% height drop per 10°C colder column yields ISA -20°C.

question_text: An aircraft flying at FL 100 from Marseille (QNH 1012 hPa) to Palma de Mallorca (QNH 1006 hPa) experiences no change to true altitude. The reason for this is that :
option_a: the air at Palma de Mallorca is warmer than that at Marseille
option_b: the air at Palma de Mallorca is colder than that at Marseille
option_c: the altimeters are erroneous, and need to be tested
option_d: one of the two QNH values may be incorrect
explanation: Marseille has a higher QNH than Palma, but Palma is warmer. The warmer air column over Palma expands to compensate for the lower pressure, keeping true altitude constant.

question_text: During a flight over the sea at FL 100 from Marseille (QNH 1012 hPa) to Palma de Mallorca (QNH 1012 hPa), the true altitude is constantly increasing. What action, if any, should be taken ?
option_a: None, the reason for the change is that the air around Palma is warmer than the air around Marseille
option_b: Have your altimeter checked, because its readings are obviously wrong
option_c: Recheck the QNH because one of the QNH values must be wrong
option_d: Compensate by heading further to the left
explanation: With identical surface pressures, the constant increase in true altitude during the flight indicates that the air around Palma is warmer than Marseille.

question_text: During a flight over the sea at FL 100 from Marseille (QNH 1016 hPa) to Palma de Mallorca (QNH 1016 hPa), the true altitude is constantly decreasing. What is the probable reason for this ?
option_a: The air at Marseille is warmer than that at Palma de Mallorca
option_b: One of the QNH values must be wrong
option_d: The aircraft is being blown off track to the left
explanation: With identical surface pressures, the constant decrease in true altitude during the flight indicates that the air at Marseille is warmer than at Palma.

question_text: During a flight over the sea at FL 135, the true altitude is 13500 feet, local QNH is 1019 hPa. What information, if any, can be gained about the air mass in which the aircraft is flying?
option_b: Its average temperature is the same as ISA
option_d: There is insufficient information to make any assumption
explanation: A high QNH of 1019 hPa would normally make true height higher. Since true height equals indicated height, the air mass must be colder than ISA.

question_text: An aircraft is flying over the sea at FL 90, the true altitude is 9100 feet, local QNH is unknown. What assumption, if any, can be made about the air mass in which the aircraft is flying ?
option_a: There is insufficient information to make any assumption
option_d: Its average temperature is the same as ISA
explanation: Without local QNH, we cannot compare the pressure datum with the true altitude to calculate the temperature deviation of the air mass.

question_text: An aircraft is flying over the sea at FL 120, with a true altitude of 12000 feet, local QNH is 1013 hPa. What assumption, if any, can be made about the air mass in which the aircraft is flying ?
option_a: Its average temperature is the same as ISA
option_d: There is insufficient information to come to any conclusion
explanation: With standard QNH (1013 hPa) and true altitude equal to indicated altitude, the average temperature of the air column is standard (ISA).

question_text: An aircraft is flying over the sea at FL 100, with a true altitude of 10000 feet, local QNH is 1003 hPa. What assumption, if any, can be made about the air mass in which the aircraft is flying ?
option_b: Its average temperature is about ISA
option_d: There is insufficient information to come to any conclusion
explanation: A low QNH (1003 hPa) would normally reduce true altitude. Since true altitude equals indicated altitude, the air mass must be warmer than ISA.

question_text: An aircraft is flying through the Alps on a very cold winter's day. The regional QNH is 1013 hPa. During the flight, you circle around a mountain at an altitude of its summit. What reading will the aneroid altimeter give, compared to the elevation of the summit?
option_a: A higher altitude than the elevation of the summit
option_b: A lower altitude than the elevation of the summit
option_c: The same altitude as the elevation of the summit
option_d: There is insufficient information to come to a conclusion
explanation: On an extremely cold day, the altimeter overreads (the air column is compressed), showing an altitude reading higher than the actual summit height.

question_text: An aircraft is flying through the Alps on a warm summer's day. The weather is fine, and there is a high pressure system in the area. During the flight, a mountain is passed at an altitude of its summit. What reading will the aneroid altimeter give, compared to the summit's elevation?
option_a: A lower altitude than the elevation of the summit
option_b: A higher altitude than the elevation of the summit
option_c: The same altitude as the elevation of the summit
option_d: There is insufficient information to come to a conclusion
explanation: On a warm summer day, the altimeter underreads (the air column is expanded), showing an altitude reading lower than the actual summit height.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-4246A)An aircraft is flying from Point A to Point B on the upper level contour chart. The altimeter setting is 1013,2 hPa. Which of these statements is correct?
option_a: The true altitude will be higher at A than at B
option_b: The true altitude will be higher at B than at A
option_c: Wind speed at A is higher than at B
option_d: Wind speed at Paris is higher than at B
explanation: Flying along a constant pressure surface from low pressure (A) to high pressure (B), the true altitude increases, so it is higher at B.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-4247A)An aircraft is flying from Point A to Point B on the upper level contour chart. The altimeter setting is 1013,2 hPa. Which of these statements is correct?
option_a: The true altitude will be higher at A than at B
option_b: The true altitude will be higher at B than at A
option_c: Wind speed at A is higher than at B
option_d: Wind speed at A and at B is the same
explanation: Flying from low pressure (A) to high pressure (B) on a constant pressure surface, true altitude increases, making the true altitude higher at B than A.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-4248A)An aircraft is flying from Point A to Point B on the upper level contour chart. The altimeter setting is 1013,2 hPa. Which of these statements is correct?
option_a: The true altitude will be higher at B than at A
option_b: The true altitude will be higher at A than at B
option_c: Wind speed at Madrid is higher than at A
option_d: Wind speed at B is higher than at A
explanation: Flying from low pressure (A) to high pressure (B) on a constant pressure surface, the true altitude increases, so it is higher at B than A.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-4249A)An aircraft is flying from Point A to Point B on the upper level contour chart. The altimeter setting is 1013,2 hPa. Which of these statements is correct?
option_a: The true altitude will be higher at B than at A
option_b: The true altitude will be higher at A than at B
option_c: Wind speed at A and at B is the same
option_d: Wind speed at B is higher than at A
explanation: Flying from low pressure (A) to high pressure (B) on a constant pressure surface, the true altitude increases, so it is higher at B than A.

question_text: You are flying at FL 200. Outside air temperature is -40°C, and the pressure at sea level is 1033 hPa. What is the true altitude?
explanation: FL 200 in ISA -15°C air reduces true height by 6% (-1200 ft), and a QNH of 1033 hPa increases it by 540 ft, giving a true altitude of 19,340 ft.

question_text: You are flying at FL 160. Outside air temperature is -27°C, and the pressure at sea level is 1003 hPa. What is the true altitude?
explanation: FL 160 in ISA -10°C air reduces true height by 4% (-640 ft), and a QNH of 1003 hPa reduces it by 270 ft, giving a true altitude of 15,090 ft.

question_text: You are planning to fly across a mountain range. The chart recommends a minimum altitude of 12000 feet above mean sea level. The air mass you will be flying through is an average 10°C warmer than ISA. Your altimeter is set to 1023 hPa (QNH of a nearby airport at nearly sea level). What altitude will the altimeter show when you have reached the recommended minimum altitude?
explanation: A true altitude of 12,000 ft in ISA +10°C air makes the altimeter underread by 4% (-480 ft), and a QNH of 1023 hPa offsets it, reading 11,520 ft.

question_text: Which of the following conditions would cause the altimeter to indicate a lower altitude than that actually flown ?
option_c: Pressure altitude the same as indicated altitude.
explanation: An air temperature higher than standard expands the air column, making the altimeter underread (indicate a lower altitude than actually flown).

question_text: The pressure altitude is equal to the true altitude if
option_b: the outside air temperature is standard for that height
option_c: the air pressure is 1013.25 hPa at the surface
option_d: the indicated altitude is equal to the pressure altitude
explanation: Pressure altitude equals true altitude under standard atmospheric conditions, where pressure is 1013.25 hPa and temperature is standard.

question_text: The following temperatures have been observed over a station at 1200 UTC. Assume the station is at MSL. Height in feet. Temperature in degrees C. 20000.-12 18000.-11 16000.-10 14000.-10 12000.-6 10000.-2 8000. +2 6000. +6 4000. +12 2000. +15 surface+15.
option_a: Assuming that the MSL pressure is 1013.25 hPa the true altitude of an aircraft would actually be higher than the indicated altitude.
option_b: The height of the freezing level over the station is approximately 12000 FT.
option_c: The temperature at 10000 FT is in agreement with the temperature in the International Standard Atmosphere.
option_d: The layer between 16000 and 18000 FT is absolutely unstable
explanation: Since the actual temperatures are warmer than standard, the air column is expanded, making the true altitude higher than the indicated altitude.

question_text: Assume that an aircraft is flying in the northern hemisphere at the 500 hPa pressure surface on a heading of 270 degrees. Which of the following statements is correct?
option_a: If in this pressure surface the wind comes from the direction 360 degrees, then true altitude is increasing
option_b: If in this pressure surface the wind comes from the direction 180 degrees, then true altitude is increasing
option_c: If in this pressure surface the wind comes from the direction 270 degrees, then true altitude is increasing
option_d: If in this pressure surface the wind comes from the direction 090 degrees, then true altitude is increasing
explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, a right crosswind (from 360° on a 270° heading) means high pressure is to the north (right), so true altitude is increasing.

question_text: An aircraft is flying at FL 180 on the northern hemisphere with a crosswind from the left. Which of the following is correct concerning its true altitude ?
option_d: Without knowing temperatures at FL 180 this question can not be answered.
explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, a left crosswind indicates flying toward low pressure, which causes the true altitude to decrease.

question_text: What is the relationship, if any, between QFE and QNH at an airport situated 50 FT below sea level?
explanation: Since QNH is station pressure reduced to MSL and the airport is below sea level, the station pressure (QFE) is greater than QNH.

question_text: An aircraft lands at an airport (airport elevation 1240 FT, QNH 1008 hPa). The altimeter is set to 1013 hPa. The altimeter will indicate :
explanation: An altimeter set to 1013 hPa in QNH 1008 hPa overreads by 135 ft (5 hPa * 27 ft), showing 1375 ft at airport elevation 1240 ft.

question_text: After landing at an aerodrome (aerodrome elevation 1715 FT), the altimeter indicates an altitude of 1310 FT. The altimeter is set to the pressure value of 1013 hPa. What is the QNH at this aerodrome?
explanation: The altimeter reads 405 ft lower than airfield elevation, indicating QNH is 15 hPa (405 / 27) higher than standard 1013 hPa, which is 1028 hPa.

question_text: An aircraft is descending to land under IFR. If the local QNH is 1009 hPa, what will happen to the altitude reading when the altimeter is reset at the transition level ?
explanation: Resetting the altimeter to transition level from standard (1013) to QNH (1009) reduces the subscale pressure, causing the reading to decrease.

question_text: After landing at an aerodrome (QNH 993 hPa) it is noticed that the altimeter is still set to 1013,2 hPa and that it reads 1200 feet. What is the elevation of the aerodrome above mean sea level ?
explanation: The altimeter set to 1013.2 in QNH 993 overreads by 540 ft (20 hPa * 27 ft). The airport elevation is 1200 - 540 = 660 feet.

question_text: During the climb after take-off, the altimeter setting is adjusted at the transition altitude. If the local QNH is 1023 hPa, what will happen to the altimeter reading during the resetting procedure ?
option_d: It is not possible to give a definitive answer
explanation: During climb, adjusting transition setting from QNH (1023) to standard (1013.2) reduces the reference pressure, causing the altimeter reading to decrease.

question_text: During the climb after takeoff, the altimeter setting is adjusted at the transition altitude. If the local QNH is 966 hPa, what will happen to the altimeter reading during the resetting procedure?
option_d: It is not possible to give a definitive answer
explanation: During climb, adjusting transition setting from QNH (966) to standard (1013) increases the reference pressure, causing the altimeter reading to increase.

question_text: An aircraft lands at an airport (airport elevation 540 FT, QNH 993 hPa) with the altimeter set to 1013 hPa. What will it indicate ?
explanation: An altimeter set to 1013 in QNH 993 overreads by 540 ft (20 hPa * 27 ft). At airport elevation 540 ft, it will read 1080 ft.

question_text: What pressure is defined as QFE?
option_c: The pressure reduced to sea level using actual temperatures
option_d: The pressure reduced to sea level using ISA temperatures
explanation: QFE is the actual atmospheric barometric pressure measured at the official airfield elevation.

question_text: An altimeter adjusted to 1013 hPa indicates an altitude of 3600 FT. Should this altimeter be adjusted to the local QNH value of 991 hPa, the altitude indicated would be
explanation: Changing subscale from 1013 hPa to 991 hPa reduces the reference pressure by 22 hPa, decreasing the indicated altitude by 594 ft to 3006 ft.

question_text: In Geneva, the local QNH is 994 hPa. The elevation of Geneva is 1411 FT. The QFE adjustment in Geneva is
explanation: An elevation of 1411 ft equals a 52 hPa correction (1411 / 27). Subtracting this from QNH 994 hPa yields a QFE of 942 hPa.

question_text: An aircraft is flying at FL 80. The local QNH is 1000 hPa. After the second altimeter has been adjusted to the local QNH, the reading will be approximately
explanation: Changing setting from standard (1013) to QNH (1000) decreases the subscale by 13 hPa, reducing the indicated altitude from 8000 ft to 7650 ft.

question_text: The barometric compensator of an altimeter is locked on reference 1013.2 hPa. The aircraft has to land on a point with an elevation of 290 feet where the QNH is 1023 hPa.Assuming that 1 hPa corresponds to 27 FT, the reading on the altimeter on the ground will be:
explanation: An altimeter set to 1013.2 at QNH 1023 underreads by 265 ft (9.8 * 27). At elevation 290 ft on the ground, it reads 20 ft.

question_text: Which of the following statements is true ?
option_a: QNH can be equal to QFE
option_b: QNH is always lower than QFE
option_c: QNH is always higher than QFE
option_d: QNH is always equal to QFE
explanation: QNH equals QFE if the airport elevation is at mean sea level (0 ft elevation), as no height correction is required.

question_text: Which statement is true ?
option_a: QNH can be lower as well as higher than 1013.25 hPa
option_c: QNH is lower than 1013.25 hPa at any time
option_d: QNH can be 1013.25 only for a station at MSL
explanation: QNH represents actual sea level pressure, which can vary higher or lower than the standard pressure of 1013.25 hPa.

question_text: When the subscale is set to the QNH of an airfield the pressure altimeter indicates
option_c: elevation while landing only if conditions are as in the International Standard Atmosphere
option_d: zero while landing only if conditions are as in the International Standard Atmosphere
explanation: When set to the local QNH, the altimeter indicates the airfield elevation above mean sea level when the aircraft is on the ground.

question_text: You must make an emergency landing at sea. The QNH of a field on a nearby island with an elevation of 4000 FT is 1025 hPa and the temperature is -20°C. What is your pressure altimeter reading when landing if 1025 hPa is set in the subscale?
option_c: More than 0 FT, but less than 4000 FT
explanation: In cold air (-20°C), pressure drops faster with height. The QNH calculated from 4000 ft is lower than actual sea pressure, making the altimeter read less than 0 ft.

question_text: The QNH is equal to the QFE if
explanation: QNH is equal to QFE when the airfield elevation is exactly zero (sea level), meaning no reduction calculations are required.

question_text: Which of the following conditions gives the highest value of the QNH?
explanation: QFE 995 hPa at 1600 ft requires a 59 hPa correction (1600 / 27), yielding the highest QNH value of 1054 hPa.

question_text: For a given airfield the QFE is 980 hPa and the QNH is 1000 hPa. The approximate elevation of the airfield is
explanation: The difference between QNH and QFE is 20 hPa (1000 - 980). Using the rule of 8 m per hPa, the elevation is 160 metres.

question_text: Before landing, an altimeter set to QFE indicates
option_a: in standard atmosphere, the height of the aircraft above the official airport elevation.
option_c: the aircraft's altitude above the mean sea level.
option_d: the height of the aircraft's wheels above the runway.
explanation: Before landing, setting the altimeter subscale to QFE causes it to indicate the height of the aircraft above the official airport elevation.

question_text: If atmospheric conditions exist such that the temperature deviation is ISA +10°C in the lower troposphere up to 18000 FT, what is the actual layer thickness between FL 60 and FL 120 ?
explanation: An indicated layer of 6000 ft in ISA +10°C air expands the column by 4% (240 ft), resulting in an actual thickness of 6240 ft.

question_text: What information is required to convert a minimum safe altitude into a lowest usable flight level?
option_a: Lowest value of QNH and the highest negative temperature deviation from ISA.
option_b: Highest value of QNH and the highest negative temperature deviation from ISA.
option_c: Highest value of QNH and the highest positive temperature deviation from ISA
option_d: Lowest value of QNH and the lowest negative temperature deviation from ISA
explanation: To determine the lowest usable flight level, the lowest QNH and highest negative temperature deviation are used to ensure the aircraft remains above the minimum safe altitude.

question_text: Which weather condition lowers true altitude as compared to pressure altitude to a position where flight over mountains could be dangereous?
explanation: A cold low pressure system reduces the spacing of pressure levels, causing the true altitude of the aircraft to be significantly lower than the indicated pressure altitude.

question_text: A vertical spacing of 1000 FT, is the standard required separation between two FL. Under conditions of cold air advection (ISA -15°C), what would the true vertical separation be?
option_d: Without QNH information, it can not be determined
explanation: Cold air advection compresses the pressure levels, meaning the true vertical separation between two flight levels will be less than the nominal 1000 feet.

question_text: At which pressure and temperature conditions may you safely assume that the minimum usable flight level at least lies at the same height, as the minimum safe altitude?
option_a: At a temperature greater than or equal to that of the ISA and where the QNH is greater than or equal to 1013 hPa
option_b: In a cold low pressure region
option_c: At a temperature less than or equal to that of the ISA and where the QNH is less than 1013 hPa
option_d: In a warm high pressure region
explanation: When the temperature is equal to or warmer than ISA and QNH is 1013 hPa or higher, the true altitude will be equal to or higher than the pressure altitude.

question_text: What is the approximate speed of a 25-knot wind, expressed in kilometres per hour?
explanation: To convert knots to kilometers per hour, multiply by 1.852. Thus, 25 knots is approximately 46.3 km/h (rounded to 45 km/h in options).

question_text: What is the approximate speed of a 90 km/h wind, expressed in knots?
explanation: To convert kilometers per hour to knots, divide by 1.852. Therefore, 90 km/h is approximately 48.6 knots (rounded to 50 knots).

question_text: What is the approximate speed of a 40-knot wind, expressed in m/sec?
explanation: To convert knots to meters per second, divide by approximately 1.94. Thus, 40 knots is approximately 20.6 m/s (rounded to 20 m/s).

question_text: What values are used for the forecasted wind at higher levels?
option_a: Direction relative to true north and speed in knots
option_b: Direction relative to magnetic north and speed in knots
option_c: Direction relative to magnetic north and speed in kmh
option_d: Direction relative to grid north and speed in kmh
explanation: Upper wind forecasts always specify wind direction relative to true north and wind speed in knots.

question_text: Whilst flying at FL 180 on the northern hemisphere an aircraft experiences right drift. What effect, if any, will this have on the aircraft's true altitude ?
option_d: Without knowing the pressure change this question cannot be answered.
explanation: Experiencing right drift in the Northern Hemisphere means the wind is from the left. This indicates flying toward low pressure, which decreases true altitude.

question_text: Which forces are balanced with geostrophic winds?
option_b: Friction force, pressure gradient force, Coriolis force.
option_c: Pressure gradient force, Coriolis force, centrifugal force.
option_d: Pressure gradient force, centrifugal force, friction force.
explanation: The geostrophic wind is a theoretical wind resulting from a balance between the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force.

question_text: In the southern hemisphere what wind effect would you expect when flying from a high pressure area towards a low pressure area at FL 100?
explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, winds blow clockwise around high pressure and counter-clockwise around low pressure, resulting in a wind from the right when flying from high to low pressure.

question_text: An aircraft flying in the southern hemisphere at 2000 feet, has to turn to the right in order to allow for drift. In which direction, relative to the aircraft, is the centre of low pressure ?
explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, wind circulates clockwise around a low pressure area, putting the center of low pressure to the left when turning right to counter drift.

question_text: The geostrophic wind is greater than the gradient wind around a low pressure system because the
option_a: centrifugal force opposes the pressure gradient
option_b: centrifugal force is added to the pressure gradient
option_c: coriolis force is added to the pressure gradient
option_d: coriolis force opposes to the centrifugal force
explanation: In a low pressure system, the centrifugal force acts outwards, opposing the inward pressure gradient force. This reduces the wind speed compared to geostrophic wind.

question_text: The geostrophic wind is less than the gradient wind around an anticyclone because the
option_a: centrifugal force is added to the pressure gradient
option_b: centrifugal force opposes the pressure gradient
option_c: effect of coriolis is added to friction
option_d: coriolis effect opposes the centrifugal force
explanation: In a high pressure system, the centrifugal force acts outwards in the same direction as the pressure gradient force, making the gradient wind greater than the geostrophic wind.

question_text: An aircraft is flying in the southern hemisphere at low altitude (less than 2000 feet) and going directly away from a centre of low pressure. What direction, relative to the aircraft, does the wind come from ?
option_a: From the left and slightly on the nose
option_b: From the right and slightly on the nose
option_c: From the right and slightly on the tail
option_d: From the left and slightly on the tail
explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, wind flows clockwise and spirals outwards from low pressure due to friction, resulting in wind from the left and slightly on the nose.

question_text: What prevents air from flowing directly from high-pressure areas to low-pressure areas ?
explanation: The Coriolis force defects air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, preventing it from flowing directly from high to low pressure.

question_text: Geostrophic wind
option_a: is perpendicular to the horizontal pressure gradient force
option_b: is directly proportional to the density of the air
option_d: veers with height if cold air is advected in the northern hemisphere
explanation: The geostrophic wind flows parallel to the isobars, which means it acts perpendicular to the horizontal pressure gradient force.

question_text: Wind is caused by
option_c: friction between the air and the ground
explanation: Wind is primarily caused by horizontal pressure differences, which create the pressure gradient force that drives air motion.

question_text: You are flying from east to west in the northern hemisphere at the 500 hPa pressure surface. Which of the following statements is correct?
option_a: If the wind is from the north you are gaining altitude
option_b: If the wind is from the south you are gaining altitude
option_c: If you have a head wind you are gaining altitude
option_d: If you have a tail wind you are losing altitude
explanation: Flying west in the NH with a north wind (right crosswind) means heading toward higher pressure, which increases the aircraft's true altitude.

question_text: Geostrophic wind is the wind when isobars are
option_a: straight lines and no friction is involved.
option_b: curved lines and no friction is involved
option_c: straight lines and friction is involved.
option_d: curved lines and friction is involved.
explanation: Geostrophic wind is defined as the wind that blows when isobars are straight lines and surface friction is negligible.

question_text: The wind tends to follow the contour lines (isohypses) above the friction layer because
option_a: the coriolis force tends to balance with the horizontal pressure gradient force
option_b: contour lines are lines that connect points with the same windspeed in the upper air
option_c: the coriolis force acts perpendicular on a line that connects high and low pressure system
option_d: the friction of the air with the earth's surface gives the airflow a diversion perpendicular to the gradient force.
explanation: Above the friction layer, the Coriolis force balances the pressure gradient force, causing the wind to flow parallel to contour lines.

question_text: The wind speed in a system with curved isobars compared to a system with straight isobars is (other conditions being the same)
explanation: In anticyclonic curvature, centrifugal force acts in the same direction as the pressure gradient force, yielding higher wind speeds than straight isobars.

question_text: The geostrophic wind depends on
option_b: earth's rotation, geographic latitude, centripetal force
explanation: Geostrophic wind speed is determined by air density, the Earth's rotation speed, and geographic latitude.

question_text: The difference between geostrophic wind and gradient wind is caused by
explanation: The difference between geostrophic and gradient wind is caused by the centrifugal force introduced by the curvature of the isobars.

question_text: The geostrophic wind speed is directly proportional to the
explanation: The speed of the geostrophic wind is directly proportional to the steepness of the horizontal pressure gradient.

question_text: For a similar pressure gradient, the geostrophic wind speed will be
option_c: the same at all latitudes north or south of 15°
option_d: equivalent to gradient wind ± thermal component
explanation: For a similar pressure gradient, geostrophic wind speed is greater at lower latitudes because the Coriolis parameter decreases towards the equator.

question_text: For the same pressure gradient at 60°N, 50°N and 40°N the speed of the geostrophic wind will be
explanation: The Coriolis parameter decreases as latitude decreases, which increases the geostrophic wind speed for a given pressure gradient at lower latitudes (40°N).

question_text: Under anticyclone conditions in the northern hemisphere, with curved isobars the speed of the gradient wind is
option_c: the same as the thermal component
option_d: proportional only to the Coriolis force
explanation: Under anticyclonic conditions, the gradient wind speed is greater than the geostrophic wind speed because the centrifugal force acts outwards.

question_text: What characteristics will the surface winds have in an area where the isobars on the weather map are very close together?
option_a: Strong and flowing across the isobars.
option_b: Very weak but gusty and flowing across the isobars.
option_c: Strong and parallel to the isobars.
option_d: Moderate and parallel to the isobars.
explanation: Very close isobars indicate a steep pressure gradient, resulting in strong winds that flow across the isobars near the surface due to friction.

question_text: Where are you likely to find the strongest winds close to the ground?
option_a: In the transition zone between two air masses
option_b: At the centre of a low-pressure system
option_c: At the centre of a high-pressure system
option_d: Where there is little variation in pressure over a large area during the winter months
explanation: Relative humidity is directly proportional to water vapor content; adding water vapor at constant temperature increases it.

question_text: Select the true statement concerning isobars and wind flow patterns around high- and low-pressure systems that are shown on a surface weather chart.
option_a: When the isobars are close together, the pressure gradient force is greater and wind velocities are stronger.
option_b: Surface winds flow perpendicular to the isobars.
option_c: Isobars connect contour lines of equal temperature.
option_d: When the isobars are far apart, crest of standing waves may be marked by stationary lenticular clouds.
explanation: Closely spaced isobars represent a strong pressure gradient force, which drives faster wind speeds.

question_text: The greater the pressure gradient the
option_a: closer the isobars and the stronger the wind
option_b: further the isobars will be apart and the weaker the wind
option_c: closer the isobars and the lower the temperatures
option_d: further the isobars will be apart and the higher the temperature
explanation: A greater pressure gradient is indicated by closer isobars and results in stronger wind speeds.

question_text: When isobars, for an area in the mid-latitudes on a weather map, are close together, the wind is most likely to be
explanation: Closely spaced isobars indicate a strong pressure gradient, which is associated with strong wind speeds.

question_text: Which of the following is true concerning an aircraft that is flying at FL180 in the northern hemisphere, where wind is geostrophic and the true altitude remains constant ?
option_b: There is a cross wind from the left
option_c: There is a cross wind from the right
option_d: Without knowing temperature at FL 180 this question can not be answered
explanation: If the geostrophic wind is parallel to the flight path and true altitude remains constant, there is no crosswind component.

question_text: In a low pressure system the convergence at the surface is caused by
option_c: the inbalance of the horizontal gradient force and the Coriolis force
explanation: Surface friction slows the wind, which reduces the Coriolis force and allows the pressure gradient force to pull the air inward, causing convergence in a low.

question_text: In an area of converging air
explanation: Air convergence at the surface forces vertical ascent, which cools the air adiabatically and leads to cloud formation.

question_text: Divergence in the upper air results, near the surface, in
option_a: falling pressure and likely formation of clouds
option_b: rising pressure and likely formation of clouds
option_c: rising pressure and likely dissipation of clouds
option_d: falling pressure and likely dissipation of clouds
explanation: Upper-level divergence pulls air upward, resulting in falling surface pressure and cloud formation.

question_text: Between which latitudes are you most likely to find the subtropical high-pressure belt ?
explanation: The subtropical high-pressure belt is located between 25° and 35° latitude in both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

question_text: Between which latitudes are you most likely to find the region of travelling low pressure systems ?
explanation: Travelling low pressure systems associated with the polar front are typically found in the mid-latitudes between 55° and 75°.

question_text: In the central part of the Atlantic Ocean between 10°N and 20°N the prevailing winds are
option_b: NE monsoon in winter and SW monsoon in summer
option_d: SW winds throughout the whole year
explanation: The tropical Atlantic between 10°N and 20°N is dominated by the northeast (NE) trade winds blowing towards the ITCZ.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-10721A)Assuming a generalised zonal system of world wind circulation, the SE trade winds are applicable to zone
explanation: According to the global circulation model, zone w in the Southern Hemisphere is dominated by the southeast (SE) trade winds.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-10722A)Assuming a generalised zonal system of world climatic and wind circulation, zone ""t"" is an area of
explanation: Zone t represents the horse latitudes, which are dominated by subtropical high-pressure systems.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-10723A)Assuming a generalised zonal system of world wind circulation the travelling low pressure systems are applicable to zone
explanation: Zones s and y represent the mid-latitude belts dominated by travelling low pressure systems and frontal activity.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-10724A)Considering Melbourne (C) in July, the weather is predominantly influenced by the zone of
option_a: subtropical high pressure, with the occasional passage of fronts originating in the adjacent zone of disturbed temperate low pressure
option_b: antarctic high pressure due to the absence of any protective land mass between south Australia and Antarctica
option_c: disturbed temperate low pressure, bringing an almost continuous succession of fronts resulting in strong winds, low cloud and rain
option_d: equatorial low pressure due to the proximity of the intertropical convergence zone over central Australia
explanation: In July (winter in the Southern Hemisphere), Melbourne's weather is predominantly influenced by subtropical high-pressure systems and passing polar fronts.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-10725A)Assuming a generalised zonal system of world climatic and wind circulation, zone ""y"" is an area of
explanation: Zone y in the Southern Hemisphere represents the mid-latitude belt of travelling low pressure systems.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-10726A)Assuming a generalised zonal system of world wind circulation, the NE trade winds are applicable to zone
explanation: Zone u in the Northern Hemisphere represents the tropical belt dominated by the northeast (NE) trade winds.

question_text: (For this question use annex 050-10727A)Assuming a generalised zonal system of world climatic and wind circulation, zone ""u"" is in area of
explanation: Zone u represents the subtropical latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere, which are dominated by the NE trade winds.

question_text: Which degree of aircraft turbulence is determined by the following ICAO description?""There may be moderate changes in aircraft attitude and/or altitude but the aircraft remains in positive control at all times. Usually, small variations in air speed. Changes in accelerometer readings of 0.5 to 1.0 g at the aircraft's center of gravity. Occupants feel strain against seat belts. Loose objects move about. Food service and walking are difficult.""
explanation: Moderate turbulence is characterized by moderate changes in attitude/altitude, small airspeed variations, and loose objects moving about.

question_text: All pilots encountering Clear Air Turbulence are requested to report it. You experience CAT which causes passengers and crew to feel definite strain against their seat belt or shoulders straps. Unsecured objects are dislodged. Food service and walking are difficult. This intensity of CAT should be reported as
explanation: CAT that causes occupants to feel definite strain against seat belts and dislodges unsecured objects is classified as moderate.

question_text: What degree of turbulence, if any, is likely to be encountered while flying through a cold front in the summer over Central Europe at FL 100?
explanation: In summer over Central Europe, cold fronts produce intense convective activity, leading to severe turbulence inside Cumulonimbus (CB) clouds.

question_text: Which cloud type may indicate the presence of severe turbulence ?
explanation: Altocumulus lenticularis clouds form in the crests of mountain waves, indicating severe turbulence and wave activity.

question_text: Fair weather cumulus often is an indication of
option_a: turbulence at and below the cloud level
option_c: smooth flying conditions below the cloud level
explanation: Fair weather cumulus clouds indicate convective thermal activity and turbulence occurring at and below the cloud base.

question_text: On a clear summer day, turbulence caused by solar heating is most pronounced
option_c: during early morning hours before sunrise
explanation: Turbulence caused by solar heating (convection) is most pronounced during early afternoon when ground temperatures reach their maximum.

question_text: Generally northern hemisphere winds at 5000 FT/AGL are southwesterly while most of the surface winds are southerly. What is the primary reason of difference between these two wind directions?
option_a: Friction between the wind and the surface.
option_b: A strong pressure gradient at higher altitudes.
option_c: Stronger Coriolis force at the surface.
option_d: The influence of warm air at the lower altitude.
explanation: Surface friction slows the wind, reducing the Coriolis force and causing the wind to back (turn left in NH) compared to the wind aloft.

question_text: Friction between the air and the ground results in the northern hemisphere in:
option_a: backing of the wind and decrease of wind speed at the surface.
option_b: veering of the wind and decrease of wind speed at the surface.
option_c: backing of the wind and increase of wind speed at the surface.
option_d: veering of the wind and increase of wind speed at the surface.
explanation: Surface friction slows the wind and reduces Coriolis deflection, causing the wind to back and decrease in speed in the Northern Hemisphere.

question_text: You are flying at 2 500 FT/AGL, with a southerly wind, and intend to land at an airport, at sea level directly below. From approximately which direction would you expect the surface wind (mid-latitude, northern hemisphere)?
explanation: Due to surface friction, a southerly wind aloft will back (turn left in the NH) at the surface, blowing from the south-southeast.

question_text: If Paris reports a wind of 19015KT on the METAR, what wind velocity would you expect to encounter at a height of 2000 feet above the ground ?
explanation: At 2000 ft, friction is negligible, so the wind will veer (turn right by ~30°) and speed will approximately double, yielding 22030KT.

question_text: If Paris reports a wind of 08010KT on the METAR, what wind velocity would you expect to encounter at a height of 2000 feet above the ground ?
explanation: At 2000 ft above the surface, the wind veers (turns right) and increases in speed, changing from 08010KT to approximately 11020KT.

question_text: If Paris reports a wind of 16020KT on the METAR, what wind velocity would you expect to encounter at a height of 2000 feet above the ground?
explanation: At 2000 ft above the surface, the wind veers (turns right) and increases in speed, changing from 16020KT to approximately 19040KT.

question_text: If Paris reports a wind of 30012KT on the METAR, what wind velocity would you expect to encounter at a height of 2000 feet above the ground ?
explanation: At 2000 ft above the surface, the wind veers (turns right) and increases in speed, changing from 30012KT to approximately 33025KT.

question_text: In the lower layers of the atmosphere due to friction the wind changes direction towards the low pressure area because :
option_a: wind speed decreases and therefore coriolis force decreases
option_c: turbulence is formed and pressure increases
option_d: turbulence is formed and pressure decreases
explanation: Friction slows surface air, which weakens the Coriolis force and allows the pressure gradient force to deflect wind toward the low pressure.

question_text: What causes surface winds to flow across the isobars at an angle rather than parallel to the isobars ?
option_c: Greater density of the air at the surface
option_d: Greater atmospheric pressure at the surface
explanation: Surface friction slows the wind, which weakens the Coriolis force and causes the wind to blow across the isobars at an angle.

question_text: In the northern hemisphere a pilot flying at 1000 FT/AGL directly towards the centre of a low pressure area, will find the wind blowing from
option_c: about 45 degrees to the right of directly ahead
explanation: In the NH, wind flows counter-clockwise and spirals inward toward a low, meaning wind blows from the left and behind when flying toward it.

question_text: In the northern hemisphere the wind at the surface blows
option_a: counter-clockwise around, and toward the centre of, a low pressure area
option_b: from a low pressure area to a high pressure area
option_c: clockwise around, and away from the centre of, a low pressure area
option_d: counter-clockwise around, and away from the centre of, a high pressure area.
explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, surface winds flow counter-clockwise and inward toward the center of a low pressure system.

question_text: During a descent from 2000 FT above the surface to the surface (no frontal passage) the wind normally
explanation: Descending to the surface, friction increases, causing the wind to back (turn left in NH) and decrease in speed.

question_text: What relationship exists between the wind at 3000 feet and the surface wind?
option_a: The wind at 3000 feet is parallel to the isohypses and the surface wind direction is across the isobars toward the low pressure and the surface wind is weaker.
option_b: They have the same direction, but the surface wind is weaker, caused by friction
option_c: They are practically the same, except when eddies exist, caused by obstacles
option_d: The surface wind is veered compared to the wind at 3000 feet and is usually weaker.
explanation: The wind aloft is parallel to the isobars, while surface friction slows the wind and causes it to blow across isobars toward low pressure.

question_text: The vertical extent of the friction layer depends primarily on
option_a: stability, wind speed, roughness of surface
option_b: wind speed, roughness of surface, temperature
option_c: roughness of surface, temperature, local time
option_d: temperature, local time, environmental lapse rate
explanation: The height of the friction layer is determined by surface roughness, wind speed, and atmospheric stability.

question_text: During periods of prolonged clear skies associated with anticyclonic conditions, the
option_a: surface wind speed tends to be highest during the early afternoon
option_b: surface wind speed tends to be highest at night
option_c: angle between isobars and surface wind direction tends to be greatest in the early afternoon
option_d: wind tends to back from early morning until early afternoon
explanation: Under clear skies, surface heating causes convective mixing in the afternoon, bringing faster wind momentum down and increasing surface wind speed.

question_text: In the northern hemisphere the gradient wind of a cyclonic pressure distribution is 350/24, over the sea the surface wind would approximate
explanation: Over the sea, surface friction is low, causing the wind to back by only ~10° and decrease in speed by ~20%, yielding 340/20.

question_text: In the northern hemisphere with an anticyclonic pressure system the geostrophic wind at 2000 FT over the sea is 060/15. At the same position the surface wind is most likely to be
explanation: Over the sea, friction causes the geostrophic wind to back by ~15° and decrease in speed by ~20%, changing 060/15 to 045/12.
